Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has pointed to breadth, the share of categories with prices rising faster than 3%, as a key indicator. 

In October, 59.3% of the 182 CPI item categories rose at a monthly pace that would exceed 3% over a full year, the most since January 2023 and up from 49.2% in September, against a 42.3% average from 2000 to 2019. 

Over three months, the share rose to 52.5%, the most since March, and over six months to 42.4%, the most since July, from 37.7%. 

Looking year-over-year, our estimate is that 52.0% of categories rose more than 3%, the most since May, up from 47.2%, or 63.8% of the basket by weight, the most since September 2025. 

The share above 5% rose to 26.0% of categories (15.8% of the basket) from 23.0%, while the share falling from a year earlier dropped to 20.8% from 27.5%.*

The S&P 500 fell 0.4% Tuesday, but the VIX also fell 2.4%, extending Monday’s 22% drop.

“Spot down, vol down” at that size is rare: just 4% of comparable S&P 500 down days since 1990, and the first since March 2025.

▪ It usually comes as fear drains after a spike: 69 of the 100 cases came with the VIX already at 19+.
▪ Seven came within three sessions of a 30%+ VIX jump, like this one, including China’s devaluation (2015), Brexit (2016) and Volmageddon (2018).
▪ The S&P 500 was higher a month later all seven times (avg. +4.2%) and three months later in six of seven (avg. +4.4%), vs. +0.8% and +2.4% for all days.
▪ The exception was 1990, ahead of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait.

Note: The VVIX also fell, but adding that to the analysis doesn't change things.

Caveat: Small sample size.

Citi’s earnings revision index was +0.02 in the week of October 30th, down from +0.06 the prior week (there was no reading the week before that), as its 20-week average continued to roll over, to about 0.16 from 0.18 two weeks earlier and 0.28 in mid-September.

As I noted on October 25th, three of the four prior rollovers of about 0.8, 0.16 and 0.1 points in the 20-week average since 2021 (Jul ’21, Jun ’24, Sep ’25) were followed by declines of 25%, 8.5% and 9.1% (in 2023 the SPX declined first). 

At the time the index was down 2.5% from its October 6th record, and I said it was still too early to tell how much further (if any) the softening had to go. As of Friday, the SPX had fallen 5.7%.

As I mentioned in last Thursday's evening update, we saw the first 80% NYSE downside volume day since December 2025, ending the longest streak without one in at least 30 years, per BTIG’s Jonathan Krinsky via @dailychartbook's nightly email.

In the 15 previous “first in 3+ months” cases since 1996 according to Krinsky's analysis:

▪ 11 saw at least one more 80% downside days within 30 sessions, and five saw five or more.
▪ The S&P 500 was lower on average one and two weeks later, and up just 0.3% a month later (higher 53% of the time).
▪ When five or more followed, it was higher 50 sessions later just once (avg. -6.9%).
▪ When fewer followed, it was higher 30 sessions later in 9 of 10 cases (avg. +3.5%).

The 30-session window runs through December 18.

Our direct experience with Nvidia, never shared before:

22 months ago, we published the below analysis raising concerns that Nvidia's AI chips were potentially being routed to China through Singapore.

Less than 24 hours later, Nvidia's Head of PR contacted us, directly addressing our analysis. Their message to us is included below.

At the time, in the previous 3 quarters, $17.4 billion of Nvidia's revenue came from Singapore versus $11.6 billion from China.

Furthermore, at the time, the US had ~5,375 data centers, China had 448, and Singapore had just 99. The numbers just did not add up. You can read our full analysis below.

Nvidia's PR team sent us the following message:

"The revenue associated with Singapore does not indicate diversion to China. Our public filings report 'bill to' not 'ship to' locations of our customers. Many of our customers have business entities in Singapore and use those entities for products destined for the US and the West. We insist that our partners comply with all applicable laws, and if we receive any information to the contrary, act accordingly. Our last 10-Q noted: 'most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.'"

Fast forward to today.

According to new reports, Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies through a network spanning China and Singapore.

The reported shipments date back to 2023 and involved ~240,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips.

These allegations remain under investigation, and it is not yet established whether the shipments were connected to the revenue discrepancies we highlighted 22 months ago.

Nvidia maintains that it has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.

But the overlap between these new allegations and the questions we raised in January 2025, along with Nvidia's response to us at the time, is noteworthy.

We stand by our view that Jensen Huang is likely to remain CEO of Nvidia and will continue to be an integral figure in the AI Revolution.

We expect more on this soon.

HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says it's less scary to build an AI startup now than in 2023, as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road the frontier labs are following:

"The frontier model companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars building, doing the pre-training. And so their whole business effectively now is taking the capex that they've spent and the money they're continuing to spend and saying, 'How do we sell inference? How do we sell tokens? How do we monetize the thing that we've built?'"

"There are SaaS companies and startups that know their particular domain, know their market, have some distribution, or have something that allows them to sell tokens and be a reseller of inference."

"Think of AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and cloud infrastructure 15 years ago... I think it's less scary now to build in and around the AI arena than it was in 2023."

"We have open source. We have lots of great commercial products. So as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road, it is completely possible now that you're not gonna get margined out, because you have options."

@dharmesh

tweets.text: Many people forget just how long the 'winter' was for $GLD. It had an initial burst, even becaming the biggest ETF in world for one day in 2011 ,and then the bad times came and and it (saw 40% of investors bail) and took nearly a DECADE to get back to its that aum high again. Today it sits at nearly 3x that initial high water mark and has tied SPX perf since launching and is considered a wildly successful ETF category. My point: assets without cash flows run purely on sentiment and it changes. To me this is the closest analog to bitcoin ETFs and how to think about them.

Most dashboards tell you what moved. The Radar on the Helios Analytics crypto terminal tells you what moved abnormally.

Every asset is scored against its own history, price and fundamentals (fees, revenue, TVL, volume), so a move is judged by how unusual it is for that coin rather than how big it looks.

That matters in a month like this one. Only 9 of 182 assets rose and the median coin fell 23%. In absolute terms almost everything looks the same. Relative to their own history, a few stand right out.

THORChain is the fundamental divergence. $RUNE revenue is +3.6 SD vs its 1-year norm, with the 14-day average up 66% in a month and at the 97th percentile of the past year. The price is down 13% over the same 30 days.

BitTorrent is the volume one. $BTT traded $39M on 9 Nov, almost double its 14-day average and +4.1 SD vs its 1-year norm, while the price barely moved (-2.5% for the month).

Neither is a buy signal on its own (a spike can be noise, or one big trade). But when the whole market is red, knowing which numbers are genuinely out of character is a much better place to start.
